content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

Transparency and oversight are essential for building trust, improving accountability, and ensuring that energy policies are fair, efficient, and effective. This lesson explores how open data, accessible information, and strong monitoring systems help prevent corruption, improve decision-making, and attract investment. It introduces key tools like internal and external audits, gender audits, and strategic foresight to strengthen public trust and ensure that no one is left behind in the energy transition.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: A: Tranparency

content.text: Thus, in addition to fostering informed decision-making and accountability, institutionalizing transparency in <ai prompt="Provide more info on energy governance.">energy governance 💬️</ai> yields several other key benefits

Transparency in energy governance rests on two key pillars.
First, it involves the availability of accurate, reliable, and timely information on energy production, consumption, and trade. This information is essential for a wide range of stakeholders, policymakers, investors, and consumers alike, as it enables informed decisions about energy investments, policy interventions, and consumption behaviors.
Second, transparency is recognized as a cornerstone of effective energy governance because it empowers stakeholders to fully understand the implications of energy decisions and to hold policymakers accountable for their actions.

content.title: Enhancing Public Trust
content.body: When institutions operate transparently, they build credibility and trust among citizens. This trust is vital for public acceptance of energy policies, especially when such policies require significant behavioral or economic adjustments from the populace.

content.title: Policy Coherence and Coordination
content.body: Transparency fosters alignment across different levels of government and sectors by making energy data, targets, and decisions openly accessible and comparable. This enables integrated planning, reduces policy conflicts, and supports coordinated action on complex issues of energy energy and ensure a more unified and effective energy transition.

content.title: Facilitating Investment
content.body: Transparent markets attract investors by reducing informational asymmetries and perceived risks. Investors are more likely to fund renewable energy projects when they have clear insights into regulatory frameworks, financial incentives, and market operations.

content.title: Promoting Efficient Resource Allocation
content.body: Transparency ensures that resources allocated for the energy transition are used effectively. It allows for the monitoring of fund disbursement and project execution, thereby minimizing waste and mismanagement.

content.title: BOX: The Green Bond Transparency Platform, Inter-American Development Bank

content.text: The Green Bond Transparency Platform (GBTP), launched in April 2021 by the Inter-American Development Bank and IDB Invest, exemplifies how transparency can drive sustainable energy investments. This platform aims to increase transparency in the green bond market, facilitating reporting and verification of green investments.

Within a year of its launch, the GBTP became the primary reporting tool for 73% of the green bond market in Latin America and the Caribbean, representing $26.8 billion in investments.
The GBTP enhances transparency by enabling issuers and external reviewers to report directly on the use of green bond proceeds and their development impacts in a secure, blockchain-enabled environment.
This ensures the integrity and reliability of data, which builds investor confidence and facilitates greater participation in the green bond market. By providing verifiable insights into the performance of sustainable energy investments, the platform shows the importance of transparency in scaling sustainable energy initiatives and demonstrates how robust governance can accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
Accessible and Understandable Information

A fundamental principle of transparent governance is the open conduct of government activities, ensuring that information is readily available and comprehensible to citizens. This encompasses providing detailed information on policy objectives, comprehensive implementation plans, and anticipated outcomes, all presented in a clear and concise manner, deliberately avoiding technical jargon and overly complex terminology.

While the importance of clear and accessible information is widely recognized, a significant challenge often arises in ensuring that this information is truly understandable to all stakeholders. Simply making raw data or complex legal documents publicly available does not equate to genuine transparency if the audience lacks the technical expertise or context to interpret it. This creates an "understandability gap" where, despite efforts to disclose information, it effectively remains opaque to a significant portion of the public. This can negate the intended benefits of information disclosure, such as informed decision-making and public scrutiny.
For transparency initiatives to be truly effective, particularly in diverse contexts like developing countries, policymakers and energy developers must invest significantly in user-friendly communication strategies. This includes developing simplified language summaries, utilizing data visualization tools, and offering educational programs to bridge the knowledge gap. Without addressing this "understandability gap," efforts to improve information accessibility will fall short of empowering citizens and fostering genuine public engagement.

Beyond mere accountability, open data can reveal unmet market needs and emerging opportunities within the energy and sustainability sectors. It can significantly improve operational efficiency (e.g., utility companies leveraging weather data for optimized grid management), accelerate research and development, and attract crucial investment by reducing perceived risks and building investor confidence.
Therefore, governments should strategically view open energy data platforms not merely as a regulatory requirement or a public service, but as critical national infrastructure that can stimulate new business models, foster a more competitive energy market, and accelerate technological adoption. For developing countries, this is particularly pertinent as it offers a pathway to bypass traditional energy infrastructure development by leveraging data-driven insights to attract investment and drive localized innovation.
Establish Open Data Initiatives and Digital Platforms

content.title: BOX: IEA’s Designing an energy statistics roadmap Assessment tool

content.text:
The IEA guidebook provides a comprehensive framework for strengthening national energy information systems, crucial for tracking progress in clean energy transitions. It addresses the need for robust, accurate, and accessible energy data to inform policy decisions, monitor efficiency, and assess emissions and renewable energy goals. Developed through consultations with countries and experts, the guidebook outlines a three-dimensional strategy for improving data collection: planning, setting up infrastructure, and tracking data quality and accessibility.

It offers practical steps and best practices, emphasizing the importance of governance, resource allocation, and innovation, such as digitization. Targeted especially at developing countries, the guidebook helps assess energy data systems, identify gaps, and create tailored action plans. By aligning with international standards, it supports transparency, governance effectiveness, and data-driven policymaking for sustainable energy transitions.

content.title: BOX: MRV tracking visualization platform in Uruguay

content.text:
During the development of its Third Biennial Update Report, Uruguay implemented a domestic Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system in the form of a database of policies and measures, relevant emissions reductions or avoided emissions, and information on adaptation, technology transfer 💬️, financing, capacity-building, and mitigation (UNDP, 2022). Also included in the system are technical sheets and methodologies that define indicators towards the implementation of different measures.

In June 2019, a visualization platform was created and made publicly available on the Ministry of Environment website to inform Uruguayan citizens of the progress made towards the goal for each measure, its contribution to the National Climate Change Policy, and the SDGs, as well as a classification on each measure’s gender sensitivity. (UNDP, 2022d)

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: B: Oversight

content.text: For oversight to be effective, it must be rooted in a well-established institutional framework that incorporates both answerability (the obligation to explain actions and provide transparency) and enforcement (taking action against violations). This framework requires clear roles for both internal mechanisms within the energy agencies and external bodies, ensuring a balanced, comprehensive approach to oversight that strengthens the integrity and efficiency of energy governance.

In energy governance, oversight refers to the systematic monitoring and evaluation of energy policies, projects, and systems to ensure they align with established objectives, regulations, and standards. It ensures transparency, accountability, and compliance, while addressing key issues such as access, affordability, and sustainability in the energy sector. Effective oversight helps identify risks, improve decision-making, and enhance the long-term outcomes of energy initiatives.
Beyond creating specific mechanisms to establish and strengthen public accountability, oversight can foster learning through evaluation and highlighting bad and good practices.
Oversight can take various forms, both internal and external, each serving different purposes and involving different actors.
The purpose of effective oversight can vary depending on the specific context:

content.title: Ensuring Policy Implementation
content.body: Oversight can ensure that energy policies are pursued efficiently and effectively, and that the resources allocated to energy projects are used appropriately.

content.title: Enforcing Accountability
content.body: Effective oversight holds energy agencies and officials accountable for their actions, ensuring they answer for their decisions and face consequences for any illegal, inefficient, or unethical conduct.

content.title: Preventing Fraud and Abuse
content.body: Oversight mechanisms, particularly those involving external actors like law enforcement agencies or auditors, help detect and prevent corruption, fraud, or mismanagement in energy-related projects.

content.text: Internal Oversight

Internal Oversight occurs within the energy governance structure itself. Agencies and organizations are responsible for monitoring their own activities to ensure compliance with policies and regulations.

For example, energy agencies may have internal units or "inspectors general" who perform independent reviews within the agency, ensuring that internal procedures are being followed, resources are properly allocated, and performance is on track. This helps maintain operational efficiency and fosters accountability within the organization. Internal oversight can also include mechanisms that encourage self-reporting of violations or mistakes.

Encouraging agencies to actively participate in oversight, rather than viewing it as an external enforcement exercise, can foster a culture of transparency and accountability. Rewards or incentives for self-reporting can motivate agencies and regulated entities to take ownership of their operations, facilitating more proactive and honest oversight.
External Oversight

This involves actors such as regulatory bodies, parliamentary committees, and independent watchdog organizations, each playing distinct roles in ensuring transparency and accountability in the energy sector.
Regulatory oversight focuses on enforcing compliance with energy laws and standards. Regulatory authorities may monitor market behavior, set tariffs, ensure fair competition, and protect consumer rights. For example, an energy regulator might investigate market abuses or mandate service quality standards, using various tools, including audits, as part of its enforcement strategy.
In parallel, external and independent audits serve as important instruments to verify financial and operational integrity. These audits, which may be conducted by independent bodies or mandated by regulators, assess whether energy companies are complying with legal and financial obligations. For instance, audits of distribution companies can uncover fraudulent practices such as “shadow employment” or misreporting of losses. While audits are sometimes initiated by regulators, they are distinct from regulatory powers and serve as a complementary accountability mechanism.
Finally, parliamentary committees or civil society watchdogs may conduct additional oversight, examining whether energy policies are being implemented as intended, whether public funds are used efficiently, and whether reforms are delivering on equity and access goals.

Gender audits are tools used to assess the extent to which gender equality is integrated into an organization’s policies, programs, and operations. They identify gaps, strengths, and opportunities to improve gender mainstreaming 💬️ and ensure that institutions or initiatives are more inclusive and equitable.

Gender audits typically evaluate institutional culture, decision-making processes, resource allocation, and the implementation of gender-related policies. Gender audits propose a more participatory approach, encouraging input from all levels of an organization to foster a collective commitment to gender equality.

This tool has evolved from being an approach to an institution’s internal evaluation of how gender equality issues were addressed in its programming to adding an external evaluation of the organization’s policies, programs and activities. In other words, it is a tool to analyze the factors that may hinder gender mainstreaming efforts in policies and in the institutions that carry out these policies.

content.title: BOX: UNDP Gender Equality Seal for Public Institutions

content.text:
The UNDP Gender Equality Seal for Public Institutions offers a framework to support and recognize public institutions that advance gender equality and women’s empowerment through a structured, voluntary certification process. Its methodology, grounded in international benchmarks, aligns well with energy transition governance, offering tools to integrate gender-responsive practices into policies and operations.

The process begins with a self-assessment to identify gender gaps, followed by an implementation plan and external evaluation for certification at bronze, silver, or gold levels.
The Seal’s five dimensions guide institutions to:

content.title: Planning and management for gender equality
content.body: Reviews the public policy cycle to ensure a gender perspective throughout the design, formulation, monitoring and evaluation phases, including analysis of human and financial resources and sex-disaggregated information systems, in the context of the 2030 Agenda.

content.title: Gender equality architecture and capacities
content.body: Examines organizational structures and horizontal and vertical coordination mechanisms, gender expertise and learning processes, leadership, external communications and knowledge management.

content.title: Work environments to enable gender equality
content.body: Analyzes and improves women's participation and access to decision-making positions, facilitating work-life balance for all and preventing gender-based violence, sexual harassment and discrimination.

content.title: Participation, partnerships and accountability
content.body: Sets the scope for improving inter-institutional coordination and partnerships with external organizations and citizen participation for gender equality in the policy cycle and accountability mechanisms.

content.title: Results and impact of public policies
content.body: Allows the public institution to showcase its efforts and results towards advancing gender equality and women's empowerment in its area of competence.

content.text: ENERGIA Gender Audit

ENERGIA, the International Network on Gender and Sustainable Energy, is recognized globally as a thought leader and a powerful voice in advancing global and national agendas for a more gender-inclusive energy sector.
ENERGIA developed a gender audit methodology tailored to the energy sector, emphasizing early involvement of Ministries of Energy to foster ownership and increase the likelihood of implementing gender-responsive energy policies.
The methodology analyzes areas such as energy planning, budgets, institutional capacity for gender mainstreaming, and the integration of gender into energy and broader national development objectives. The audits identify critical gender gaps in policy formulation and implementation, examining how gender issues are addressed by institutions and policies
Key steps include data collection (desk reviews, interviews, and focus group discussions), which inform a roadmap to enhance gender capacity, assess energy policies, and develop a gender action plan (GAP). A participatory validation workshop finalizes the process, setting specific targets and timeframes for gender integration and securing the Ministry’s commitment to the findings.

content.title: Case Study: Indonesia
content.subtitle: Applying Strategic Foresight in Performance Audit: Case Study of Audit of Energy Transition in Indonesia

content.text: Indonesia has met its growing energy demands, driven by rapid economic expansion. However, this growth has led to an unsustainable energy mix, heavily reliant on fossil fuels such as coal and oil, which contributes significantly to the country’s carbon footprint (PwC, 2024). Currently, 87% of Indonesia’s electricity comes from fossil fuels, renewables contributed only 12% in 2023, with coal accounting for 67% of power generation, making Indonesia one of the top 10 global carbon emitters, not only due to fossil fuel combustion but also for the deforestation and peatland degradation (Green Central Banking, 2025).

As climate change impacts Indonesia, the country faces an increasing risk of droughts and coastal flooding, underscoring the need for a transition to low-carbon energy sources. In response, the BPK has introduced a performance audit using strategic foresight methods. This approach goes beyond evaluating past performance to focus on anticipating future risks, identifying emerging challenges, and recommending proactive actions.

The audit followed a six-step strategic foresight framework that involved collaboration with key national stakeholders, including ministries, regulators, and the state-owned utility PLN, to gather data, validate scenarios, and align with national energy policies. Expert input guided the scanning and forecasting phases, although engagement with civil society and local actors was limited (Wibowo & Ahmad, 2024). The steps included:

Framing: Identifying strategic issues, such as how energy policies intersect with national development goals, emissions targets, and the three pillars of the energy trilemma: security, affordability, and sustainability.
Scanning: Gathering information on trends, risks, and uncertainties, including technological advancements, regulatory changes, climate risks, and global energy dynamics.
Forecasting: Developing scenarios to explore potential outcomes based on various assumptions, such as increased renewable energy investment or the phasing out of subsidies.
Visioning: Defining desirable future states for Indonesia’s energy system, including cleaner grids, equitable access, and resilient infrastructure 💬️.
Planning: Producing recommendations for government ministries on improving policy design, coordination, and risk management.
Acting: Developing a monitoring plan to track the implementation of recommendations through follow-up audits and dialogues with relevant agencies.

Despite its technical sophistication, the audit process remained largely government-centered and did not fully incorporate gender-disaggregated data, civic engagement mechanisms, or analysis of how energy reforms might affect marginalized groups. These are areas for improvement in future audits.

According to Wibowo & Ahmad (2024), the audit produced several critical findings, reshaping Indonesia’s national dialogue on energy transition:

Risk of subsidy escalation: As renewable electricity production increases, fixed tariffs could lead to rising subsidy burdens unless pricing reforms are implemented to address this issue.
Unclear financing for coal retirement: Although policies aim to reduce coal use, no dedicated funding mechanism or cost-benefit analysis has been established for the early retirement of coal-fired plants.
Dependence on imported technology: Approximately 70-80% of solar components used in Indonesia are imported, exposing the country to supply chain vulnerabilities and limiting local economic benefits.
Delayed infrastructure development: Slow progress in transmission and distribution projects has created regional disparities in electricity access and reduced power supply reliability during the transition.
Lack of social and gender analysis: No structured assessment was conducted to examine who might be excluded from or disproportionately affected by the transition, particularly women, youth, and low-income communities.

These findings reveal gaps in Indonesia’s energy governance, emphasizing that technical foresight alone is insufficient. Without inclusive perspectives and community engagement, such audits risk reinforcing top-down planning approaches that fail to serve vulnerable groups.
Moreover, Indonesia’s experience demonstrates that integrating strategic foresight into public audits can be a powerful tool for identifying blind spots and designing more resilient energy strategies. However, it also underscores the limitations of technocratic planning if social inclusion is not prioritized from the outset.
To replicate this model in other countries, several conditions are necessary:
Political support with foresight and accountability is essential.
Dedicated teams within audit institutions trained in foresight methods.
Access to cross-sectoral data and collaboration with technical ministries.
Mechanisms for civic engagement and gender inclusion in planning are important.
Countries that rely heavily on fossil fuels, such as Indonesia, often face coordination challenges and have dispersed geographies, making it difficult for them to implement long-term energy transition strategies effectively. Strategic foresight in energy auditing enables governments to anticipate future risks, enhance inter-agency coordination, and develop adaptive policies that respond to evolving energy needs. This approach also enhances public accountability by ensuring that energy transition plans are socially and institutionally viable.

takeaways.title: Effective oversight in energy governance requires both internal and external mechanisms to ensure transparency and accountability. Internal oversight encourages agencies to self-monitor and report issues, while external oversight, through regulatory bodies, parliamentary committees, and independent audits, provides checks and balances to prevent fraud and inefficiency.

Independent audits and regulatory scrutiny strengthen energy governance by detecting mismanagement, fraud, and inefficiencies. Transparent and well-conducted audits, such as those reviewing energy distribution companies, play a crucial role in uncovering corrupt practices and improving operational integrity.

Transparency builds public trust and attracts investment. Open access to accurate, timely, and understandable energy data enables accountability and informed participation.It reduces corruption risks, empowers stakeholders, and increases investor confidence in sustainable energy markets.
